title: How do you create a custom annotation (`@interface`), what are the meta-annotations (`@Retention` — SOURCE/CLASS/RUNTIME, `@Target` — METHOD/FIELD/TYPE/PARAMETER etc., `@Inherited`, `@Documented`, `@Repeatable`), and why does `@Retention(RUNTIME)` matter (allows reflection-based processing by frameworks)?
shortTitle: How do you create a custom annotation?

s1_definition.profdef: A custom annotation is declared with the `@interface` keyword and defines named elements that look like methods, each of which can have a default value. Meta-annotations are annotations that annotate the annotation itself to control its behavior. `@Retention` sets how long it is kept: SOURCE discards it after compilation, CLASS keeps it in the bytecode but not at runtime, and RUNTIME keeps it available for reflection. `@Target` restricts where it may be applied, such as METHOD, FIELD, TYPE, or PARAMETER. `@Inherited` lets a class annotation be seen on subclasses. `@Documented` includes it in Javadoc. `@Repeatable` allows applying it more than once on the same element. `@Retention(RUNTIME)` matters because only runtime-retained annotations are visible to reflection, which is how frameworks like Spring, JPA, and JUnit discover and act on them.
s1_definition.analogy: A custom annotation is like designing a new official rubber stamp for the bank, where you decide what information the stamp records, like a risk level, and give sensible defaults. The meta-annotations are the rules printed on the stamp's handle: one rule says how long the stamp's mark should survive, whether it fades after the form is typed up, stays only in the archive copy, or remains clearly readable forever so an auditor can scan it later. Another rule says where the stamp is allowed, only on account forms or only on signature lines. Another says whether a stamp on a parent file automatically applies to child files. The survive-forever setting is the crucial one, because the bank's automated scanners, the frameworks, can only react to stamps that are still readable at scan time.
s1_definition.oneliner: Declare a custom annotation with @interface and control it with meta-annotations, and use @Retention(RUNTIME) so reflection-based frameworks can actually see and act on it.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A custom annotation is declared with the `@interface` keyword and defines named elements that look like methods, each of which can have a default value. Meta-annotations are annotations that annotate the annotation itself to control its behavior. `@Retention` sets how long it is kept: SOURCE discards it after compilation, CLASS keeps it in the bytecode but not at runtime, and RUNTIME keeps it available for reflection. `@Target` restricts where it may be applied, such as METHOD, FIELD, TYPE, or PARAMETER. `@Inherited` lets a class annotation be seen on subclasses. `@Documented` includes it in Javadoc. `@Repeatable` allows applying it more than once on the same element. `@Retention(RUNTIME)` matters because only runtime-retained annotations are visible to reflection, which is how frameworks like Spring, JPA, and JUnit discover and act on them.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** A custom annotation is like designing a new official rubber stamp for the bank, where you decide what information the stamp records, like a risk level, and give sensible defaults. The meta-annotations are the rules printed on the stamp's handle: one rule says how long the stamp's mark should survive, whether it fades after the form is typed up, stays only in the archive copy, or remains clearly readable forever so an auditor can scan it later. Another rule says where the stamp is allowed, only on account forms or only on signature lines. Another says whether a stamp on a parent file automatically applies to child files. The survive-forever setting is the crucial one, because the bank's automated scanners, the frameworks, can only react to stamps that are still readable at scan time.

**One line to remember:** Declare a custom annotation with @interface and control it with meta-annotations, and use @Retention(RUNTIME) so reflection-based frameworks can actually see and act on it.

sections.s2_technical:
You declare a custom annotation with `@interface`, and its body contains elements that look like abstract methods but act as named attributes. For example `@interface Audited { String action(); RiskLevel risk() default RiskLevel.LOW; }` defines a mandatory action element and an optional risk element with a default. Element types are limited to primitives, String, Class, enums, other annotations, and arrays of those. An element named `value` is special because it can be supplied without naming it, so `@Audited("TRANSFER")` works if value is the single element.

`@Retention` is the single most consequential meta-annotation. SOURCE means the annotation exists only in the source and the compiler discards it, which suits things processed at compile time like Lombok or Override. CLASS, the default, keeps it in the class file but the JVM does not load it, suitable for bytecode tools. RUNTIME keeps it in the class file AND makes it available through reflection at runtime, which is the only level at which frameworks can read it while the program runs. If you forget to set RUNTIME on an annotation that a framework must read reflectively, the framework will simply not see it, and the feature silently does nothing, which is a very common beginner mistake.

`@Target` restricts the program elements the annotation may be placed on, using the ElementType enum with values like TYPE for classes and interfaces, METHOD, FIELD, PARAMETER, CONSTRUCTOR, LOCAL_VARIABLE, and ANNOTATION_TYPE. For example `@Target(ElementType.METHOD)` means it can only annotate methods, and misusing it elsewhere becomes a compile error, which documents intent and prevents wrong placement. Without a Target the annotation may be used almost anywhere.

The remaining meta-annotations refine behavior. `@Inherited` applies only to annotations on classes and makes a subclass report the annotation as present even though it is declared only on the superclass, which matters when reflection walks class annotations; it does not apply to methods or interfaces. `@Documented` causes the annotation to appear in the generated Javadoc of the annotated element, which is useful for API-facing markers. `@Repeatable` allows the same annotation to be applied multiple times on one element by declaring a containing annotation, for example applying several `@Schedule` annotations to one method. Reading annotations reflectively uses the reflection API: `method.getAnnotation(Audited.class)` returns the instance if present and runtime-retained, `isAnnotationPresent` tests presence, and `getAnnotationsByType` handles repeatables.

Why RUNTIME retention matters in practice is the heart of the question. Frameworks work by scanning classes and members with reflection and reacting to annotations: Spring finds beans by component annotations and wires methods by request-mapping annotations, JPA maps entities and columns by entity and column annotations, Jackson controls JSON by its property annotations, and JUnit discovers tests by the test annotation. Every one of these relies on the annotation being retained at RUNTIME, because reflection can only report annotations that are present in the loaded class metadata. A senior engineer stresses that you choose retention by who consumes the annotation: SOURCE for compile-time code generators and linters, CLASS for bytecode-weaving tools, and RUNTIME for anything read by a running framework, and that building your own small annotation processor, whether a runtime reflective scanner or a compile-time processor, is a common senior task for cross-cutting concerns like auditing and validation.
sections.s3_banking:
National Bank of India needed a lightweight auditing marker so that sensitive operations are logged uniformly, and a custom runtime annotation read by a small reflective scanner fit perfectly, while also teaching the retention lesson.

Problem 1 — the team wanted to mark certain service methods as audited and attach an action name and a risk level, which is exactly a custom annotation with a mandatory and a default element.

Problem 2 — the first attempt forgot to set RUNTIME retention, so the reflective scanner found nothing and no audit logs appeared, even though the annotation was clearly present in the source. This is exactly why @Retention(RUNTIME) matters for reflection-based processing.

Problem 3 — the annotation was accidentally placed on a field where it made no sense, so the team added a method target to restrict it, and they wanted the marker to show in Javadoc, requiring documented.

The fix declares an Audited annotation with RUNTIME retention, a method target, and documented, then a small reflective AuditScanner reads it from a service's methods and logs the action and risk before invoking. The code defines an `Account`, a `RiskLevel` enum, the `Audited` annotation, a `TransferService` with an audited method, and an `AuditScanner` that uses reflection. The demo scans and runs an audited transfer from Rajesh to Priya.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a TransferService with one method annotated Audited with action FUNDS_TRANSFER and risk HIGH, and one unannotated method, plus a transfer of forty-five thousand from Rajesh to Priya.

Step 1. The Audited annotation is declared with RUNTIME retention, a method target, and documented. The RUNTIME retention is the crucial choice, because it means the annotation is stored in the class metadata and remains visible to reflection while the program runs. The method target restricts it to methods so it cannot be misapplied to a field.

Step 2. The scanner's scan method uses reflection to list the service's declared methods and checks each for the Audited annotation with isAnnotationPresent. It finds the transfer method, reads the annotation instance, and logs its action FUNDS_TRANSFER and risk HIGH. It ignores the unannotated balanceOf method. This only works because the annotation is runtime-retained; with SOURCE or CLASS retention, reflection would report nothing.

Step 3. The invokeAudited method looks up the transfer method by name and signature, reads its Audited annotation, and because it is present logs an audit record with the action and risk before invoking. This is exactly how a framework interposes behavior based on an annotation.

Step 4. The reflective invoke calls the real transfer method, which debits Rajesh and credits Priya by forty-five thousand, so Rajesh falls to nine hundred fifty-five thousand and Priya rises to two hundred ninety-five thousand.

Step 5. The demo logs the discovered audited method, the audit record, the transfer, and the updated balances, demonstrating a complete custom-annotation plus reflective-processor flow and making the retention lesson concrete, since omitting RUNTIME would have produced no audit output at all.

Final output:

```
2026-10-30 19:21:10 [INFO] Found audited method transfer action=FUNDS_TRANSFER risk=HIGH
2026-10-30 19:21:10 [WARNING] AUDIT action=FUNDS_TRANSFER risk=HIGH invoking transfer
2026-10-30 19:21:10 [INFO] transfer 45000.00 SAV2001 -> CUR3001
2026-10-30 19:21:10 [INFO] Rajesh=955000.00, Priya=295000.00
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  ── Declare custom annotation ──
  @Retention(RUNTIME) @Target(METHOD) @Documented
  @interface Audited { String action(); RiskLevel risk() default LOW; }

  ── Apply ──
  TransferService.transfer(...)  ◄── @Audited(action="FUNDS_TRANSFER", risk=HIGH)
  TransferService.balanceOf(...) ◄── (no annotation)

  ── Reflective scan (works ONLY because retention = RUNTIME) ──
  AuditScanner.scan(TransferService.class)
       │ for each method: isAnnotationPresent(Audited)?
       ├─ transfer  → getAnnotation → action=FUNDS_TRANSFER, risk=HIGH log
       └─ balanceOf → not present → ignored
       ▼
  invokeAudited(service,"transfer",...)
       │ read @Audited → log AUDIT record
       │ method.invoke(service, rajesh, priya, 45000)
       ▼
  transfer executes → Rajesh 955000.00, Priya 295000.00

  ── Retention contrast ──
  SOURCE  → discarded after compile → reflection sees NOTHING
  CLASS   → in bytecode, not loaded → reflection sees NOTHING
  RUNTIME → in class metadata       → reflection SEES it (frameworks work)
```

sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — Custom Annotation & Meta-Annotations ═══

  ┌─ Design Decisions ────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  @Retention(RUNTIME): reflection/frameworks can read it.        │
  │  @Target(METHOD): restrict placement, document intent.          │
  │  @Documented: marker appears in Javadoc for API users.          │
  │  value element + defaults for ergonomic usage.                  │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── Meta-annotation roles (as prose) ───────────────────────────
  @Retention: SOURCE (compile-time only) / CLASS (bytecode, default) /
    RUNTIME (reflective). @Target: where it may apply (METHOD, FIELD, TYPE...).
  @Inherited: class annotation seen on subclasses. @Documented: Javadoc.
  @Repeatable: apply multiple times via a containing annotation.

  ── Class Diagram ───────────────────────────────────────────────

  ┌──────────────────────────────┐        ┌─────────────────────┐
  │  <<annotation>> Audited      │        │     RiskLevel       │
  │  @Retention(RUNTIME)         │───────▶│  LOW, MEDIUM, HIGH  │
  │  @Target(METHOD) @Documented │  uses  └─────────────────────┘
  │  + action(): String          │
  │  + risk(): RiskLevel = LOW   │
  └──────────────┬───────────────┘
                 │ applied to
                 ▼
  ┌──────────────────────────────┐        ┌─────────────────────┐
  │       TransferService        │◄───────│    AuditScanner     │
  │  + transfer(...) @Audited    │ reflects│ + scan(Class)       │
  │  + balanceOf(...)            │  on     │ + invokeAudited(...) │
  └──────────────────────────────┘        └─────────────────────┘

  ── Call Chain ──────────────────────────────────────────────────
  1. scan(TransferService.class) → getDeclaredMethods → isAnnotationPresent
  2. transfer → getAnnotation(Audited) → log action/risk
  3. invokeAudited(service,"transfer",...) → read @Audited → log AUDIT
  4. method.invoke(...) → transfer executes

  Contract for scan(type):
    Pre:  Audited must be @Retention(RUNTIME) to be visible
    Post: logs every @Audited method's action and risk
    Trap: SOURCE/CLASS retention → reflection finds nothing (silent no-op)
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
A custom annotation is declared with the at-interface keyword, and its body defines named elements that look like methods, each of which can have a default value. The element types are limited to primitives, String, Class, enums, nested annotations, and arrays of those, and an element named value is special because it can be supplied without naming it. Meta-annotations are annotations that annotate my annotation to control its behavior.

The meta-annotations are Retention, Target, Inherited, Documented, and Repeatable. Retention sets how long the annotation is kept: SOURCE discards it after compilation for things like compile-time code generators, CLASS keeps it in the bytecode but the JVM does not load it, suitable for bytecode tools, and RUNTIME keeps it in the class metadata and makes it visible to reflection at runtime. Target restricts where the annotation may be applied, such as method, field, type, or parameter, and misuse becomes a compile error. Inherited lets a class-level annotation be reported on subclasses, Documented includes it in Javadoc, and Repeatable allows applying it more than once on the same element through a containing annotation.

Why Retention RUNTIME matters is the heart of it. Reflection can only report annotations that are present in the loaded class metadata, so only runtime-retained annotations are visible at runtime. Every framework that works by scanning and reacting to annotations depends on this: Spring discovers beans and wires request mappings, JPA maps entities and columns, Jackson controls JSON, and JUnit discovers tests, all by reading runtime-retained annotations reflectively. If I forget RUNTIME on an annotation a framework must read, the framework simply does not see it and the feature silently does nothing, which is a very common mistake.

In our auditing feature at National Bank of India, I built a custom Audited annotation with a mandatory action element and an optional risk element with a default, and I annotated it with Retention RUNTIME, a method Target, and Documented. A small reflective scanner reads Audited from the service methods and logs the action and risk before invoking, which is a miniature version of what Spring AOP does at scale. Our first attempt forgot RUNTIME retention and the scanner found nothing even though the annotation was right there in the source, which taught the team the retention lesson firsthand. We added the method target after the annotation was once misplaced on a field, and Documented so the marker shows up in the API Javadoc. The rule I apply is to choose retention by who consumes the annotation: SOURCE for compile-time processors, CLASS for bytecode tools, and RUNTIME for anything read by a running framework.

---

keyPoints: @interface MyAnnotation { String value(); int count() default 0; }
@Retention(RUNTIME): available via reflection at runtime — most common
@Retention(SOURCE): discarded by compiler, @Retention(CLASS): in bytecode only
@Target(METHOD/TYPE/FIELD): restricts where annotation can be applied
Spring, JPA, JUnit all depend on RUNTIME retention for their annotations
